references.text: The immediate context: one of Jesus' disciples cut off the ear of the high priest's servant with a sword ([ref:Luk 22:49-50|Luke 22:49-50]). Jesus intervenes and heals the injury, showing his mercy even in the midst of his own arrest.

In Matthew's parallel account, Jesus commands the disciple to put the sword back into its sheath and says that those who take up the sword will perish by the sword ([ref:Matt 26:51-52|Matthew 26:51-52]). Jesus rejects the use of violence for his own defense.

John identifies the disciple as Peter and the servant as Malchus, and records Jesus' words to put the sword back into its sheath ([ref:Joh 18:10-11|John 18:10-11]). Luke is the only one who mentions that Jesus healed the ear.
Mark's brief parallel account states that one of those standing there drew his sword and cut off the ear of the high priest's servant ([ref:Mark 14:47|Mark 14:47]).

Jesus' teaching to love your enemies and do good to those who hate you ([ref:Luk 6:27-28|Luke 6:27-28]). By healing the ear of his enemy's servant, Jesus lives out his own command to love one's enemies.
Jesus' command to love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you ([ref:Matt 5:44|Matthew 5:44]). The healing of the high priest's servant is a concrete example of this teaching in practice.
Jesus touches the bier of the dead young man and raises him up ([ref:Luk 7:14-15|Luke 7:14-15]). Another example where Jesus heals by touch, just as he here touches the ear and heals the servant.
Jesus touches the leper and heals him ([ref:Luk 5:12-13|Luke 5:12-13]). Healing through physical contact is a recurring feature of Jesus' miracles.

The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant: "By his wounds we have been healed" ([ref:Jes 53:5|Isaiah 53:5]). Jesus heals others even as he himself is about to be handed over to suffering and death.
Paul urges not to repay evil with evil, but to overcome evil with good ([ref:Rom 12:17-21|Romans 12:17-21]). Jesus' action at his arrest is the prime example of this attitude.

Peter writes that Christ did not repay insult with insults when he was insulted, nor threaten when he suffered, but entrusted himself to him who judges justly ([ref:1 Pet 2:23|1 Peter 2:23]). Jesus' reaction at his arrest illustrates exactly this.
